title: Relational Calculus
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs use TRC to check whether candidates understand declarative querying and that relational calculus and relational algebra have the same expressive power.

phases.goal: Establish what Tuple Relational Calculus is and how it differs from relational algebra.

must_hit.point: TRC is a non-procedural (declarative) query language: it specifies what data to retrieve, not how to execute the retrieval.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts TRC with procedural relational algebra and says TRC states the desired result without naming an operation sequence.

must_hit.point: A TRC expression has the form {t | P(t)}: the set of all tuples t for which predicate P(t) is true.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes or describes the set-comprehension form with a free tuple variable and a predicate.

must_hit.point: Predicates are built from atomic attribute/constant comparisons combined with OR (∨), AND (∧), and NOT (¬), plus existential and universal quantifiers over relations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the three connectives and mentions ∃/∀ as the way to quantify over tuples in relations.

probes: What is Tuple Relational Calculus, and how does a TRC query differ from a relational-algebra expression?

hints.1: Think about whether the language tells you the steps or only the result condition.
hints.2: Recall the set form that binds a tuple variable to a predicate built from comparisons, connectives, and quantifiers.
hints.3: TRC is declarative: {t | P(t)} is the set of tuples satisfying P, unlike relational algebra which sequences operators.

phases.goal: Establish how quantifiers and safety constrain what a TRC query may return.

must_hit.point: ∃ t ∈ r (Q(t)) means there exists a tuple t in relation r such that Q(t) is true; ∀ t ∈ r (Q(t)) means Q(t) is true for all tuples t in r.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states both quantifiers with the “exists in r” / “for all in r” readings.

must_hit.point: An expression is unsafe if it can produce an infinite relation; systems therefore restrict queries to safe expressions whose results come only from the database domain (constants in the database relations or in the query).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate links finiteness/computability to restricting results to the finite database domain rather than an open-ended universe.

must_hit.point: Domain Relational Calculus binds variables to single attributes (domains) rather than entire tuples, and shares the same expressive power as TRC and relational algebra.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says DRC is the variable-per-attribute cousin of TRC and notes equal expressive power with TRC and RA.

probes: What do the existential and universal quantifiers mean in TRC, and when is a TRC expression considered unsafe?

hints.1: Separate the meaning of ∃/∀ from the separate issue of whether the result set is finite.
hints.2: Existential asserts some matching tuple in a relation; universal asserts the condition for every tuple; safety limits results to the database domain.
hints.3: ∃ t ∈ r (Q(t)) / ∀ t ∈ r (Q(t)) as above; unsafe queries can be infinite (e.g. names of non-suppliers), so only safe expressions over the database domain are allowed.

phases.goal: Establish that TRC, DRC, and relational algebra differ in form but not in expressive power.

must_hit.point: Relational algebra is procedural (dictates the sequence of operations); TRC is declarative (states what to retrieve without defining how).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate clearly assigns procedural vs declarative to RA vs TRC.

must_hit.point: Despite different paradigms, TRC and relational algebra have the exact same expressive power: any query in one can be translated into the other.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate asserts equivalence of expressive power and mutual translatability, not superiority of one language.

must_hit.point: DRC vs TRC is attribute/domain variables versus whole-tuple variables; DRC has the exact same expressive power as TRC and relational algebra.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts binding granularity and again states equal power across DRC, TRC, and RA.

probes: How do relational algebra, tuple relational calculus, and domain relational calculus compare in style and expressive power?

hints.1: Separate surface style (how you write the query) from what queries you can express.
hints.2: RA sequences operators; TRC/DRC use predicates—DRC per attribute, TRC per tuple—then ask whether power differs.
hints.3: RA is procedural, TRC declarative, DRC attribute-variable; all three have the exact same expressive power and are inter-translatable.

phases.goal: Formulate TRC queries over Supplier, Parts, and Catalog, including multi-relation existential patterns.

must_hit.point: Basic TRC retrieval projects attributes under membership and conditions, e.g. {S.name | Supplier(S)} and {P.name | Parts(P) ∧ P.color = 'Red'}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes a set comprehension with the free tuple in the target relation and AND for attribute filters.

must_hit.point: Suppliers who supplied some part use an existential over Catalog linked by Sid: {S.Sid | Supplier(S) ∧ ∃ c(Catalog(c) ∧ c.Sid = S.Sid)}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate introduces ∃ c over Catalog and equates c.Sid with S.Sid (Sname variant only changes the projected attribute).

must_hit.point: Suppliers of some red part nest existentials through Catalog into Parts, checking pid equality and P.color = 'Red'.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate nests ∃ c and ∃ p, joining Sid then pid, and constrains part color to 'Red'.

probes: Using Supplier, Parts, and Catalog, write a TRC query for the names of suppliers who supplied some red part.

hints.1: You need a path from Supplier through the linking Catalog relation into Parts.
hints.2: Existentially quantify a catalog tuple matching Sid, then a parts tuple matching pid with color 'Red', and project S.name.
hints.3: {S.name | Supplier(S) ∧ ∃ c(Catalog(c) ∧ c.Sid = S.Sid ∧ ∃ p(Parts(p) ∧ p.pid = c.pid ∧ p.color = 'Red'))}.

tradeoffs.topic: Relational Algebra vs Tuple Relational Calculus
tradeoffs.strong_answer: RA is procedural and sequences operations; TRC is declarative and uses {t | P(t)}. They have the exact same expressive power, so any query in one translates into the other.

tradeoffs.topic: Tuple Relational Calculus vs Domain Relational Calculus
tradeoffs.strong_answer: TRC binds variables to whole tuples; DRC binds variables to single attributes/domains. DRC has the exact same expressive power as TRC and relational algebra.

gotchas.trap: Treating {s.name | ¬Supplier(s)} as a valid query for “everyone who is not a supplier.”
gotchas.correction: That expression is unsafe: the domain of names is theoretically infinite, so the result can be infinite. Restrict to safe expressions whose results come only from the database domain.

gotchas.trap: Assuming TRC is more or less powerful than relational algebra because it is declarative.
gotchas.correction: Paradigm differs, but TRC and relational algebra have the exact same expressive power and are mutually translatable.
